To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) type 2 diabetes is a global health problem with increasing incidence in low- and medium-income countries; (2) the main drivers of the global diabetes epidemic are the nutrition transition and the increasing burden of overweight and obesity; and (3) dietary interventions that focus on improving carbohydrate intake quality may help prevent type 2 Diabetes.
the global epidemic of diabetes is a result of a nutrition transition, and that the dietary interventions to prevent this disease must be based on the local context and culture.

1) a high-carbohydrate quality diet, with emphasis on the intake of whole grain, legumes and non-processed fruit, is associated with a lower risk of type 2 DM and 2) the dietary guidelines for diabetes prevention and management should emphasize the importance of whole grain, vegetables and legumes as a replacement of refined grains and sugars.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of diet, particularly the quality and quantity of carbohydrate, on the development of type 2 DM and the metabolic syndrome.
understanding the role of diet and nutrition in the prevention and management of diabetes.
the effects of diet on the health of the individual.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no single food or nutrient that is the ‘magic bullet’ for the prevention of type 2 DM.
there is no single dietary pattern that can be recommended to all populations.
the evidence is not yet conclusive on the role of carbohydrate quality in the development of diabetes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we need to better understand the role of dietary carbohydrates in the global burden of diabetes and that we need to implement culturally relevant and effective dietary interventions to prevent and control type 2 diabetes.
the nutrition transition is a major driver in the increasing global burden of type diabetes, and that dietary interventions to prevent and control diabetes are feasible in many settings.
the nutrition transition has been associated with an increasing prevalence of type 2 DM worldwide.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the global nutrition transition is a major contributor to the global epidemic in type 2 diabetes and that dietary interventions that target carbohydrate quality are a key component of a comprehensive strategy to prevent and control type 2 diabetes.

dietary interventions that focus on improving the quality of carbohydrates in the diet may have a greater potential to prevent and manage type 2 diabetes, especially in populations undergoing the nutrition transition, than interventions that focus on weight loss alone.
the nutrition transition is an important driver of the global diabetes epidemic.
